What gravity does for you

You opened a repo and found a .gravity/ folder. This page explains what it is, how far it reaches, and what to say to an agent to get the most out of it.

The companion file .gravity/GRAVITY.md is the same protocol written for the agent — compact and canonical. This page is written for you. If the two ever disagree, the card wins.

01What this is

Gravity is a documentation protocol. It is a small set of rules about which document owns which fact, so that you — and an AI agent working in this repo — can find the one thing that matters without reading everything, and can change it without breaking something three files away.

It is not a framework, not a dependency, and nothing in your build depends on it. It is a handful of file conventions plus a few stdlib-only Python scripts that check whether the conventions still hold. Delete the folder and the code still compiles; you just lose the map.

The one idea worth carrying into everything below: every fact has exactly one home, and every other document links to it rather than restating it. A fact written in two places eventually becomes two different facts, and nobody can tell which one is true.

Two audiences, deliberately. Files ending .md here are written for the agent — compact, scannable, cheap to load. Files ending .html (this one, MISSION.html, ARCHITECTURE.html) are written for you — browser-read, generous, and never auto-loaded, so their length costs the agent nothing. The same split runs all the way down: a domain's SPEC.md is the short contract an agent loads before a change; its ARCHITECTURE.html is the full reasoning you read when you want to understand it.

02The problem it solves

Ask an agent to change something in an unfamiliar codebase and there are three ways it goes wrong. Two of them are about reading, and one is about writing.

Dashed and solid carry the meaning, not the colour alone — the same rule every mark on these pages follows.

The third failure is quieter and worse: you did write it down, in three places, and they have since drifted apart. Now the agent reads a rule that used to be true. Documentation that lies is more expensive than no documentation, because it is trusted.

Gravity's answer to all three is the same: give every fact one owner, and make the path to the right facts short enough that reading it is cheaper than guessing.

03Four clocks, not one README

A single README mixes facts that change at wildly different speeds. The fast-moving half ("we're mid-way through the auth refactor") rots the slow-moving half ("this exists to give analysts a searchable archive"), and after a few months the whole file reads as untrustworthy. So gravity splits by rate of change.

DocAnswersRead it when
MISSION.htmlWhy — the north star, the principles, the things deliberately not builtyou are deciding whether something belongs at all
CLAUDE.mdHow — identity, stack, run and test commands, entry points, gotchasalways; it auto-loads for the agent
IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.mdWhat next — phases, locked decisions, the current gateyou are picking up the arc, not just a task
CONTEXT.mdNow — current state and exactly one next stepfirst thing every session; it auto-loads too

Only two of these are ever required: CLAUDE.md and CONTEXT.md. Everything else in gravity — including this page — is recognized when present and never mandated. A CLI with one script does not need a mission statement, and gravity will not nag it for one.

CONTEXT.md is a snapshot, not a log. It holds present reality and one next step. It is not a diary, because git log -p CONTEXT.md already recovers every past version verbatim — so pruning it is non-destructive. If you find yourself appending, you are duplicating git.

04The map — domains and the _ sigil

When a project outgrows four flat files, the heavy documents move into .gravity/ and group by subject domain — not by document type. The folder already names the subject, so the files inside are named by kind.

.gravity/
  GRAVITY.md              # the protocol card — the canon, for the agent
  GRAVITY.html            # this page — the same protocol, for you
  ROUTER.md               # THE MAP of this project: what to read before changing what
  MISSION.html            # why · ARCHITECTURE.html — how · IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md — what next
  _lib/                   # the installed instruments (machine-managed, never hand-edited)
  _observatory/           # generated output — git-ignored; regenerate it, never fix it
  _inbox/                 # the drop zone: put a received file here, then ask to route it
  _given/                 # received evidence, with a provenance manifest
  _roadmap/               # the plan sheet + the stakeholder engagement book
  <domain>/   ARCHITECTURE.html · SPEC.md · PLAN.*.md
  integration/  SPEC.md   # the contracts BETWEEN domains and services

Two rules make that tree readable at a glance:

A leading _ marks gravity's own machinery — never a subject domain. That is why _lib/ and _observatory/ sort away from your real domains instead of hiding among them, and why nothing can accidentally mint a domain called lib. Within the family there is one distinction worth knowing: _observatory/ is generated and ignored by git, while _given/ and _roadmap/ are authored and committed.

Not every feature is a domain. A domain is a durable subject an agent will navigate and change repeatedly — it has its own principle, its own rules worth fencing, and an arc longer than one pull request. A feature that fails that test is a PLAN.*.md under an existing domain, not a new folder. Work that spans several domains is work in them, not a new one. The cost of a folder is that four indexes must learn about it, so the gate is deliberately hard to pass.

Start with the map, always. This page describes the protocol in general. .gravity/ROUTER.md describes this project: which domains exist and which document to read before changing each one. It is the single most useful file in the folder, and it is the one you should open next.

05SPECs are walls, not wishes

A domain's SPEC.md is the short document you hand an agent before it changes that domain. It has two halves that do opposite jobs: a Minimal Shape to build from, and a set of Rules that fence what may not break.

The part that keeps it honest is that every rule carries an enforcement tag saying what would actually catch a violation:

TagMeans
[lint] [type]a linter or the type-checker fails if you break it
[test:name]that named test fails — the strongest tag, because it points at a run you can do right now
[review]nothing mechanical catches this; a human has to notice
[—]nothing enforces it at all. It is a convention, and it says so

The tags exist because the alternative is worse. A rule list where everything reads equally authoritative invites an agent — and you — to assume the build will catch a mistake it cannot see. Under-claiming is the rule: when it is not clear that a rule is enforced, it gets tagged [review], never upgraded on optimism. A SPEC that admits three of its rules are unenforced is more useful than one that implies all twelve are.

A SPEC also carries a Gate: line — the one command that must pass before a change to this domain ships. It is named in the document rather than remembered, so "did you run it?" has an answer you can check rather than recall.

Behavior earns its wall — it is never granted one. A new expectation enters as given/when/then intent in a slice's PLAN. It is promoted into the SPEC's Behavioral Contract only once a named test asserts it. That promotion is called graduation, and the reason it is a ritual rather than an edit is that rewording a wish into a rule is exactly how a document starts lying: the sentence gains authority without anything gaining the ability to catch a violation.

When a change crosses a boundary — an API shape, a generated client, an auth flow, a queue, a schema shared by two runtimes — integration/SPEC.md is loaded first, then the affected domain's SPEC. It owns the Boundary Map and the change order, which is the answer to "if I change this side, what has to change with it, and in what sequence".

06How far it reaches — the whole arc

This is the part that is hard to see from the file listing. Gravity does not stop at "documents describing code" — it covers the path from a sentence somebody said in a meeting all the way to a verified line in a report you hand back to them. Three doors let outside reality in, and everything downstream keeps a citation to where it entered.

The three doors are the same door from three directions. A bug report is a scenario that is currently false and should be true. An agreed requirement is a scenario that is desired in the future. Handed-in knowledge is neither — it is the evidence you reason from. All three land as cited text before anything is planned, which is why a claim made six weeks later can always be traced back to who said it and when.

Everything after the doors exists to stop two specific lies:

  • "We designed it." The design gate is mechanical: a chunk of work cannot start while it still has open questions attached to it. Each question resolves into a dated decision with a name against it. That ledger is the analysis-and-design phase, visible to people who do not read code.
  • "It works." A report may only say verified when it can name the proof — a dated walkthrough, a green gate run, a demo somebody watched. With no proof it shows a dashed not yet verified, and no wording is allowed to dress that up. Delivered-but-unverified is the single most valuable line in any status report, so it is never the embarrassing one.

One thing the arc deliberately refuses to do: it never cuts work up in advance. Roadmap chunks stay chunk-sized — the units a stakeholder agreed to — and are only broken into slices at the moment work actually starts on them. Plans made months early are wrong in detail, and a plan that is wrong in detail is worse than one that is honest about its grain.

07The phrasebook — what to say

Gravity is used by asking for it. There is nothing to run to "activate" it. Below are the asks that get the most out of a project set up this way — say them in your own words; the point is what you are pointing the agent at.

You want to…Ask for thisYou get back
get oriented in an unfamiliar repo"Read .gravity/ROUTER.md, then tell me what this project is for and where it currently stands."an orientation off the four docs, not a guess from filenames
change one area safely"I want to change X — load the SPEC for the domain that owns it before you touch anything."the wall gets read before the code gets edited
change something that spans services"This touches both sides of the API. Load integration/SPEC.md first, then the affected domain SPECs."the change order, so the two sides cannot drift apart
add a feature"Is this a new domain, or a slice under an existing one? Walk the gate."a verdict with reasons — most features are slices
know what to read before a risky change"Assemble the read-first packet for this domain, including anything coupled to it."a short reading list plus the runnable gate for that area
deal with a batch of bug reports"Triage these: keep the reporter's wording, then find root causes."a dated sheet; no reproduction means no work item, deliberately
hand in a document, export, or schema"I put files in .gravity/_inbox/ — route them."filed evidence with provenance rows; nothing later cites a ghost
turn a customer meeting into a plan"Analyze this requirements document against the domain system."a cited analysis, roadmap chunks with estimates, and the question list for your next meeting
know what is actually proven"Run the checks and the gate, then show me what is unverified."findings and a gate result rather than reassurance
report outward"Add this cycle to the engagement book."one HTML file, evidence-bound badges, earlier deliveries untouched
resume work"Read CONTEXT.md and continue from the next step."continuity without re-explaining the project
end a session well"Update CONTEXT.md before you stop."state and one next step, ready for whoever opens it next

Three habits make all of these work better:

  • Name the area, not the file. "the search domain" routes better than a path — the router will find the files, including ones you did not know existed.
  • Ask for the wall before the work. "Load the SPEC first" costs one file read and prevents the class of mistake that is expensive to find later.
  • Ask what would catch it. "Which of these rules is actually enforced?" turns a confident answer into a checkable one.
If this repo lives in a Kepler workspace. The workspace that authored gravity also carries slash-command shortcuts for most of the rows above — /preflight, /intake, /given, /urd, /report, /patch-slice, /observatory. Those live with the workspace, not in this repo, so a clone elsewhere will not have them. The protocol works either way, because the asks above are what the commands were shorthand for.

08What is checked mechanically

The instruments live in .gravity/_lib/ and travel with the repo. They are standard-library Python with no install step, so they run in a clone that has never seen the workspace they came from:

# from the project root
python .gravity/_lib/check_project.py            # do the docs still match the repo?
python .gravity/_lib/run_gate.py --all           # run this project's real test/lint gate
python .gravity/_lib/generate_observatory.py     # one HTML page: state, drift, queue, seams
python .gravity/_lib/scan_project.py             # the raw facts the others are built on

What the checks actually prove, stated narrowly on purpose:

CheckProvesDoes not prove
consistencythe domains on disk and the indexes that list them agreethat any of them is described correctly
specan enforcement tag names something that exists in the repothat the rule is a good rule
archevery file path anchored in a diagram still resolvesthat the arrow between two boxes is right
givenevery cited piece of evidence was really handed in and filedthat the evidence is accurate

That gap is the point. A green check means the bookkeeping is intact, never the design is correct — and no status mark may be upgraded just because a checker passed. Judgment stays yours.

09What gravity does not do

  • It is not a tracker. No tickets, no burndown, no assignees, no percent-complete. Those tools exist and are better at it; duplicating them here would create a second version of the truth that instantly starts drifting from the first.
  • It does not estimate. One deliberate exception: the roadmap sheet produced from an agreed requirements document carries effort figures, because a stakeholder agreement needs them. Even there, every number is tagged with its basis — measured, derived from size drivers, or an outright guess — and figures with different bases are never added together into one confident-looking total.
  • It does not write your code or replace review. It makes an agent's reading list short and correct. What gets written is still yours to judge.
  • It never migrates judgment silently. When the protocol itself is upgraded, mechanical changes are applied and anything requiring a decision is reported to you, not quietly rewritten.
  • It does not mandate documents. Two files are the floor. Every other document here is recognized when present and absent without complaint — an empty domain folder is not a warning, it is a project that did not need one.

If a document here contradicts the code, the document is the bug. Say so, and fix it in whichever file owns that fact — exactly one does.
